procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but the case likely originated with an order dated 27.02.2009, presumably from a tax authority or tribunal, regarding income tax.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 11.05.2012 of the High Court of Delhi in ITA Nos. 1411 of 2009, ITA Nos. 967 and 968 of 2011.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondent challenged the order dated 27.02.2009 before the High Court by filing three Income Tax Appeals (Nos. 967 of 2011, 1411 of 2009 and 968 of 2011). The High Court allowed the appeals and held that the Respondent is entitled to claim deduction on the income earned from the ICDs for the relevant period under consideration under Section 80-IA of the IT Act.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Revenue (likely the Income Tax Department) appealed to the Supreme Court, being aggrieved by the High Court's judgment and order dated 11.05.2012. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's decision.

directions: The parties to bear cost on their own.

issue.issue_text: Whether the judgment of the High Court calls for any interference.

facts: The case involves an appeal against a High Court judgment concerning an income tax deduction under Section 80-IA of the IT Act for the Assessment Years 2003-04 to 2005-06.
The respondent (the taxpayer) had claimed a deduction based on a notification issued by the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) which entitled them to the benefit for 10 successive assessment years.
Subsequently, a legislative amendment removed the CBDT's power to issue such notifications.

The appellant (the Revenue) argued that this amendment nullified the earlier notification, making the respondent ineligible for the deduction for the years in question (which were after the amendment).
The High Court had sided with the respondent, allowing the deduction.
law: The central legal principle is the effect of a legislative amendment on actions validly taken under the law as it existed before the amendment.
If a legislative amendment is silent on its effect on prior, validly executed actions (like the issuance of a notification), those actions are presumed to remain valid and effective.
For a prior valid action to be nullified, the legislature must explicitly state its intention to do so in the amending text.
application: The Supreme Court analyzed the appellant's argument that the amendment, which took away the CBDT's power, rendered the earlier notification ineffective for the assessment years after 2002-03.

The Court found this argument unconvincing because the amendment was "silent" about its effect on notifications that had already been issued by the CBDT in the "legitimate exercise of the power" conferred upon it at the time.
The Court reasoned that if the legislature had intended to nullify these pre-existing notifications, it would have explicitly included such a provision in the amendment.
In the absence of such explicit language, the Court concluded that the notifications issued before the amendment remained valid and continued to have effect for their full term.
Therefore, the respondent was entitled to the deduction for the 10-year period granted by the original notification, which covered the assessment years under appeal.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court's judgment was correct and did not require interference. The reasoning was that the legislative amendment did not retroactively invalidate the notification on which the respondent's claim was based. Since the notification was valid when issued and was not nullified by the subsequent amendment, it remained in effect, entitling the respondent to the tax deduction. Accordingly, the appeal was dismissed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the judgment of the High Court calls for any interference.
appellant_arguments: The High Court was wrong in placing reliance on the Notification dated 01.09.1998 issued by the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT).
A subsequent legislative amendment meant that notifications issued earlier by the Board would cease to have effect after the Assessment Year 2002-03.
respondent_arguments: The High Court rightly set aside the judgment of the Tribunal.
Once the Inland Container Depots (ICDs) were validly notified by the CBDT, the subsequent removal of the Board's power to issue such notifications does not invalidate the existing notification.

Under the relevant Section as it stood when the notification was issued, the Respondent was eligible for a deduction for 10 successive assessment years, which covers the years under appeal (2003-04 to 2005-06).
The judgment of the High Court does not call for any interference.

statutes.act_name: Notification dated 01.09.1998 issued by the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT)

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A legislative amendment that is silent regarding its effect on previously issued notifications does not nullify those notifications, provided they were issued in the legitimate exercise of power. If the legislature intended for such notifications to cease having effect, it would have to be explicitly stated in the amendment.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A tax benefit granted for a fixed period under a validly issued notification does not cease to have effect merely because a subsequent legislative amendment removes the issuing authority's power to grant such benefits, especially when the amendment is silent on its effect on pre-existing notifications and vested rights.
legal_tests_applied: Principle of statutory interpretation that legislative intent to give retrospective effect to an amendment and nullify existing rights must be explicit, and silence on the matter implies no such effect.

Doctrine of vested rights, which holds that a benefit or exemption granted for a specific period cannot be curtailed by a subsequent amendment unless the new law explicitly requires existing beneficiaries to fulfill new conditions.
why_appellant_lost: The legislative amendment that removed the Board's power to issue notifications was silent with regard to any effect it would have upon the notifications issued earlier by the Board in due exercise of its power.
Had it been the intention of the legislature that the notifications issued by the Board earlier are of no effect after 2002-03, it would have had found a place in the said amendment.
why_respondent_won: The Respondent was held entitled to the benefit of Section 80IA of the IT Act much before the Finance Act, 2001 came into force, and this exemption for a period of 10 years cannot be curtailed or denied by a subsequent amendment.

The benefit could only be denied if the subsequent amendment specifically provided that the benefit from 01.04.2002 onwards shall only be claimed by the existing eligible units if they fulfill the new conditions, which it did not.

Notifications which were issued in legitimate exercise of the power conferred on the Board would not cease to have effect after the Assessment Year 2002-03 in the absence of express legislative provision to that effect.
policy_considerations: An exemption granted for a fixed period of 10 years cannot be curtailed by a subsequent amendment regarding eligibility conditions, as this would undermine the certainty and stability of vested rights granted under the law.
